articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
A few weeks back, this site (and indeed this reporter) excitedly covered the news that Severance was back, baby. A cryptic tweet from showrunner Ben Stiller indicated that third-season shooting had begun, in the first bit of good news for fans since the brilliant second season ended on March 20 last year.

But is the show really back? The problem is that shooting and post-production take a lot of time. Even if everything goes perfectly to plan, we’re looking at a third-season launch in fall 2027 at the absolute earliest, more than two and a half years after the second one arrived.

For comparison, the first five seasons of The Sopranos were released across a span of 1,883 days; at that point, we’ll still be months short of Stiller’s team releasing their third, and with fewer episodes per season (13 each for The Sopranos vs 9 and 10, respectively, for the first two seasons of Severance ). And even a show as superb as Severance simply isn’t worth that kind of wait.

The joy of TV is its connectedness, the way it allows you to follow a story across multiple instalments as the narrative builds and breathes. Your experience of one episode informs your response to the next. Your memories of earlier seasons make the events in later seasons matter.

Think about the bombshells that landed in later seasons of Game of Thrones (eight seasons across nine calendar years), and how much less we would care about those characters and their fates if we hadn’t lived through dozens of previous episodes alongside them.

Think about the montage sequence at the end of The Wire (five seasons across seven years) and how much its emotional force depends on everything that’s come before. And then think about how difficult it was to even remember what was going on when you sat down to watch Severance season 2 more than a thousand days after the first season finished.

There were reasons for that gap. The Covid pandemic, which had delayed the first season, was still a factor while filming the second. There were also actors’ and writers’ strikes to contend with. On top of that, the show wasn’t officially renewed for a second season until a couple of days before the first finished airing, so perhaps the team wasn’t sure where they stood or ready to get started right away.

It was never going to be an easy job turning around another season for the following year. But surely the third season ought to have been less of a challenge, given the absence of Covid and the show’s obvious status as an Apple flagship.

Ben Stiller / X

It might seem unfair to compare Severance, a streaming hit of the 2020s, with the prestige cable dramas of the 2000s and 2010s. So let’s focus on other Apple properties.

Pluribus dropped its brilliant first season in November 2025 and was promptly renewed for a second, but essentially nothing has been heard since. When questioned this month, creator Vince Gilligan sighed heavily and said it was going to be a long time. Late 2027 seems optimistic; 2028 may be more realistic. Dark Matter wrapped up its first season on June 26, 2024, and is returning for its second season on August 28.

The Morning Show, one of the only original Apple TV+ shows, is on an almost perfect two-year cadence. Even sitcom Ted Lasso, which wrapped up season 3 on May 31, 2023, only just kicked off its fourth season a couple of weeks ago.

In the case of Pluribus, as Gilligan explained, the show is a challenge from both a narrative and a logistical point of view. That’s almost certainly true of Dark Matter. And Ted Lasso wrapped up its original story in season 3, so a longer delay is understandable. But taking your time isn’t free. It costs something, particularly when you’re part of the zeitgeist. Pluribus was embedded in the culture, and the culture has moved on. Memes have a short memory.

Now consider Slow Horses, whose return for a sixth season was officially announced this month. That show is almost the polar opposite of Severance, having achieved a phenomenal rate of more than one season per year. And this pays off. The characters remain in the viewer’s mind between seasons–and when one returns, as in the new trailer, it can be played as a shocking reveal.

You don’t need a lengthy recap when referring to the twists and turns of previous seasons. I don’t think the writing of Slow Horses is anywhere near as complex as that of Severance, but the show as a whole works better because it maintains a solid release rate.

Ben Stiller, if he stumbled across this article, would probably retort that the superior qualities of his show are a direct result of taking more time over each season (and that Slow Horses has the advantage of adapting a series of books). I couldn’t entirely disagree with that, although there’s plenty of evidence to show you can make a classic TV show within time constraints and without direct source material.

Look at ER, which made one season a year, like clockwork, for 15 years. Look at its spiritual successor, The Pitt, which has happily dropped into the same pattern. It can be done without compromising on quality.

Granted, there is something very appealing about saying to creators, “Please, take your time, and make it as close to perfect as you possibly can. There’s no rush.” I absolutely get the beauty of that idea. But the reality is that at some level, beyond a certain point, there is always a rush: If you wait too long, even the most loyal of viewers will forget and move on. Apple TV deserves better than that.

articles.title: Big Walk: A Good Hang with Friends
articles.subtitle: I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: This mod transforms Doom into a terrifying tactical shooter, and it's partly inspired by another PC gaming classic
articles.subtitle: Blackout makes Doom slower, deadlier, and throws in a Crysis-style energy suit for good measure.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
It takes a brave soul to ask the question "What if Doom was an incredibly slow-moving tactical shooter?" In fact, it's not a question I ever thought I'd want an answer to—we aren't exactly short of grim-faced, hyper-lethal first-person shooters these days. But the most recent footage of Blackout has convinced me that tactical Doom might be a good idea, if only because its dark and dangerous demo looks so darned terrifying.

Blackout is a work-in-progress mod built for Doom source ports Zandronum and UZDoom, currently available in playable alpha. Created by modder PKmX, it's designed to provide "tactical military simulation-based gameplay that focuses on slow methodical clearing", according to a breakdown posted on the ZDoom forums, with players expected to "hide behind covers and execute proper breaching techniques to maximise chances of survival."

The mod makes several radical changes to Doom's basic playstyle. Movement is much slower, while your character is significantly more fragile. Weapons are based on real-life firearms that feature ADS and reloading, with damage and recoil that reflects their calibre, fire-rate, and so forth.

The enemies you face remain classic Doom monsters, but PKmX says their behaviours have been "tweaked to suit tactical gameplay". Attacks are deadlier but take longer to charge, and they can both suppress you and be suppressed by you. There's also a stealth and awareness system where gunfire draws monsters to your location, while remaining quiet may enable you to sneak past enemies unseen.

In motion, Blackout reminds me a lot of Stalker, with relatively slow movement but highly reactive (and vicious) gunplay. Surprisingly though, this isn't the inspiration that PKmX cites. Apparently, Blackout draws significantly from Crysis, right down to featuring an energy suit inspired by Crytek's nanosuit.

Not only does this feature a damage-absorbing energy shield and an "adrenaline system" that provides a speed boost when near death, but it also includes a cloaking device which temporarily makes the player "almost undetectable" by enemies.

I think this goes a long way to explain why Blackout looks as good as it does. While Blackout is clearly a more methodical shooter than Doom, the emphasis remains on action and combat rather than the strategy and resource management layer of other tactical shooters. Indeed, a commenter on PKmX's video asks whether the game will feature magazine management, to which the modder responds "one of the goals of this mod is to avoid becoming an inventory simulator."

If you fancy giving Blackout a go yourself, you can download it via the Doomworld forums. PkmX also recommends several other mods to enhance the experience, including a palette mod to make levels darker, which certainly seems to fit with Blackout's tone.

articles.title: You don’t need a new Mac. You need a new keyboard
articles.subtitle: Macworld How much time do you spend in front of your Mac every day? If it’s more than an hour or two, there’s one upgrade you can make that will transform your experience in an instant: a mechanical keyboard.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
How much time do you spend in front of your Mac every day? If it’s more than an hour or two, there’s one upgrade you can make that will transform your experience in an instant: a mechanical keyboard. This simple change can step up your productivity and make typing the most comfortable it’s ever been.

Take it from me. I’ve been using and reviewing Mac-friendly mechanical keyboards for years. I’d never go back to Apple’s Magic Keyboard, never mind any of the thousands of cheap and nasty rubber-dome alternatives that flood the market.

It really is something you have to feel to understand. Once you do, you’ll never look back. The mechanical hype is real. Here’s why you should make the switch.

Pure typing bliss

As the name suggests, a mechanical keyboard is defined by the mechanical switches that lie underneath its keycaps. Each time you press a key, it moves downward on a spring-loaded mechanism, sends a signal to macOS, then moves back up.

Conversely, on a standard keyboard such as Apple’s Magic Keyboard, the keycap sits atop a rubber dome. As you push the key, it moves downward onto the dome, which squishes down and actuates the key press.

There are several problems with this rubber dome system. The first is durability. The soft dome wears down over time, reducing the consistency of its interaction with the keyboard’s contact points and potentially introducing errors in your typing. The longer you use it, the less dependable it becomes.

Keychron Q6 Max

A mechanical switch, on the other hand, is made from much more solid metal or plastic that is designed to last. Some mechanical keyboards go a step further and use magnetic connections (based on Hall effect or tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) tech) to actuate each key press, reducing the number of physical contact points and increasing durability exponentially.

In other words, mechanical keyboards tend to be far more reliable in the long term, meaning fewer frustrating mistakes and costly replacements.

The second issue with rubber dome keyboards–the most important one–is the typing feel. Mechanical switches come in all sorts of shapes and sizes, from those that feature a tactile bump as you press the key to those that are entirely smooth in action. That’s important, because the switch you choose can have a big impact on the typing feel.

As someone who types all day, every day, I love a tactile switch because it provides physical feedback that helps me type with greater speed and accuracy than a non-mechanical keyboard ever could. For my use case, the difference between a tactile switch and a linear one–never mind a rubber dome keyboard–is night and day.

Many mechanical keyboards let you swap out the switches on the fly, giving you many different typing experiences that can be customized to your needs. You’ll never get that with a rubber dome keyboard, where you have to stick with its (often unsatisfying) under-finger feel through thick and thin.

A new world to explore

Mechanical keyboards have benefits. But aren’t they just for PC gamers? And what about the price? They’re all eye-wateringly expensive, right?

SM1 Slim Mechanical Backlit Bluetooth Keyboard

I used to think that mechanical keyboards were just for Windows users whose idea of tasteful computer design was a blinding array of garish neon lights. But while that’s the stereotype, it’s far from the truth.

These days, many manufacturers are making Mac-specific mechanical keyboards. There are excellent offerings from the likes of Logitech, Keychron, NuPhy, Satechi, and more. Lofree has a superb range of Mac keyboards color-matched to the MacBook Neo, while Corsair even collaborated directly with Apple to create the K65 Plus, which is often on sale for under $120 and well worth the price.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

articles.title: Craig Federighi and Greg Joswiak talk Siri AI and more in new interview [Video]
articles.subtitle: On the heels of Apple’s WWDC keynote this week, Greg Joswiak and Craig Federighi sat down with Laurie Segall on the Mostly Human podcast.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
On the heels of Apple’s WWDC keynote this week, Greg Joswiak and Craig Federighi sat down with Laurie Segall on the Mostly Human podcast. During the conversation, Federighi and Joz talked in-depth about Apple’s new Siri AI and Apple Intelligence announcements, the company’s broader approach to AI, and more.

I really enjoyed this explanation from Federighi about Apple’s approach to AI and why he thinks it’s totally reasonable that some people are spooked by how fast things are moving right now:

I think that AI, in Apple’s view, can be used as this incredibly empowering thing. But there is a sense that, for one, things are changing very fast in ways that I think it’s hard for any normal person to keep up with. There’s uncertainty about where does this all lead?

And while I think we can look at this as yet another thing of the scale of the Industrial Revolution, which changed our world in a giant way, that displaced a lot of people in the process and still occurred over like 80 years. And now this is happening in a compressed time frame. And so I think it’s fair for people to say, “Wow, I’m not quite certain what this is going to mean for me.

” And if you’re a student and you’re thinking, “Did I study the right thing? Is the job that I thought was the skill that I thought was going to be useful? Is that the one that’s going to be useful now that AI is quickly learning all of these things? ” I think those are all reasonable thoughts to have. You know, we’re in California. We’re optimists.

We’re trying to do the right thing where we can play the right role in our sense. And I do think in the end, this all has a happy ending, but I can certainly relate to people who say, “Wow, this is a big change. ” I mean, honestly, at this moment in time, there’s no bigger place where there’s that change than in software engineering.

It’s literally the first job that AI is showing that it can do to an incredible degree. And so everyone who works in my organization is saying, “Wow, this thing does a lot of things that I used to take a lot of pride in spending decades learning to do well, and it already does it well. articles.title: HBO Max's R-Rated 116-Minute Action Sci-Fi Sequel Is Officially a Streaming Smash Hit
articles.subtitle: Can the appeal of Karl Urban make Mortal Kombat 3 happen? The Mortal Kombat franchise has always had its ups and downs over the past 35 years, both in video game form — see Mortal Kombat: Special Forces, for example — and in live-action adaptations.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Can the appeal of Karl Urban make Mortal Kombat 3 happen?

The Mortal Kombat franchise has always had its ups and downs over the past 35 years, both in video game form — see Mortal Kombat: Special Forces, for example — and in live-action adaptations. The original Mortal Kombat movie from 1995 is still beloved by fans for its faithfulness to the source material.

But that was quickly followed by the notoriously awful Mortal Kombat Annihilation, which put the film franchise on ice for more than 20 years. 2021's Mortal Kombat movie reboot was greeted warmly by action movie fans, though some hardcore MK heads took issue with the movie's original character, Cole Young.

Warner Bros.' Mortal Kombat reboot was a huge hit on streaming, partly because the film debuted on HBO Max the same day it hit movie theaters. The success of Mortal Kombat begat a sequel, which Warner Bros. had high hopes for. Mortal Kombat 2 debuted in movie theaters in May 2026, but whatever streaming success its predecessor had didn't translate to the box office.

Mortal Kombat 2 ended its theatrical run with a $129 million gross — not exactly a "flawless victory" considering the film's reported $80 million production budget. A planned Mortal Kombat 3 is now up in the air.

But after landing on HBO Max in July, Mortal Kombat 2 has become a certified streaming hit. Mortal Kombat 's direct sequel is currently the No. 1 streaming movie on HBO Max by a wide margin, according to FlixPatrol. MK2 's revival on streaming could change the fortunes of the live-action Mortal Kombat film franchise.

When Polygon spoke to Mortal Kombat 2 director Simon McQuoid in July, he said that it was too early to tell if we'd get a Mortal Kombat 3. "It's almost like Mortal Kombat 2 hasn't had its full life cycle yet," McQuoid said ahead of the movie's home video and streaming releases. "So I think let it have its full life cycle and then, um, ask me in a few months. [laughs]"

That said, McQuoid and screenwriter Jeremy Slater were intentional about leaving doors open for a sequel.

"It's kind of what we did in the first [ Mortal Kombat ], like, don't get overconfident," McQuoid said. "The audience tells you if there [should be] another one. Don't get cocky about it and do what's right for the characters. That's always been the goal all along: Do whatever's right for the truth of the characters." Mortal Kombat 2 ended with a handful of cliffhangers that still need to be resolved.

Mortal Kombat 2 debuted in movie theaters on May 8 and opened to $48 million at the domestic box office. Ultimately, the movie went on to make $79.7 million domestically and $49.7 million internationally, according to Box Office Mojo. Warner Bros. released the film digitally on June 9, and a physical release (on 4K UHD, Blu-ray, and DVD) arrived on July 28.

articles.title: MacPaw is building an on-device AI layer that will work across your Mac apps
articles.subtitle: MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac. The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac.

The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.

MacPaw is teaming up with Liquid AI to bring more on-device AI to the Mac

Liquid AI’s Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) will be adapted for Mac-based assistance and combined with MacPaw’s own on-device technologies: Mnemos for memory and Elix for inference.

Eney already shifted to a local model last year, keeping reasoning, contextual search, skill execution, and conversation history on the device whenever possible.

The new partnership is intended to push that approach further. The two companies are jointly developing the underlying stack rather than MacPaw simply adding another third-party model.

Once the technology has been tested and implemented in Eney, MacPaw says it plans to bring it to more of its products. It also wants to make the shared AI stack available to Mac developers through Setapp.

That could let participating apps expose more of their capabilities and context to Eney. This would allow the assistant to understand what is inside an app. It could also provide more useful answers or take relevant actions.

articles.title: Siri demos in keynote were a little slow, but that’s good-ish news
articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: GTA 6 Leak and Wolverine Rage Are Symptoms of Gaming's Summer of Hate
articles.subtitle: Gamescom and the September deluge can't come soon enough Patch Notes is a weekly newsletter bringing you the best of Polygon, sent on Fridays and published on the site on Sundays. You can subscribe here.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Gamescom and the September deluge can't come soon enough

Patch Notes is a weekly newsletter bringing you the best of Polygon, sent on Fridays and published on the site on Sundays. You can subscribe here.

Man, it's been a rough summer, but I promise you, it's nearly over.

It has always been like this. For decades, the game industry has more or less shut down — or reduced itself to a small hum of subsistence — between the noisy previews of E3/Summer Game Fest in early June, and the noisy previews of Gamescom in late August. People go on vacation, players spend more time outside, and there are few big games released. Then Gamescom fires the starting gun on the busiest release period of the year.

It's never been quite like this, though. This year, releases slowed down but the news cycle didn't. We had the Xbox layoffs, Sony killed physical games. Everyone was hot and angry. The gulf between the number of exciting new games to play and talk about and the number of enraging topics to consume the discourse just kept growing. The algorithms must be fed, after all, even if it's only with bitter gruel.

This week, gaming's summer stumbled to an exhausted climax with the Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks, which started out fun and, like everything else, quickly turned awful.

Patricia Hernandez reported on the leaker's apparent activist motivation on Tuesday…

…but by Wednesday, that narrative was already starting to unravel

By Friday, Ashely Claudino was reporting that the leaker's real motivation may be a crypto get-rich-quick scheme

Yuck. Not that anyone should really expect a hacker to be a moral paragon. This is theft, after all. The leaker began by channelling gamers' anger at Rockstar over the lack of a physical edition of GTA 6. Meanwhile, they have also generated an equal amount of sympathy for a studio — however monolithic — that is just trying to finish its magnum opus and having its hard work spoiled by bland videos of an out-of-date build.

Rockstar will be infuriated, but it's more insult than injury

Rockstar will be fine, of course, as I pointed out in my analysis above. But the whole thing leaves a bad taste in the mouth. The leaker exploited the lull in the gaming calendar, and they exploited Rockstar's iron grip on GTA 6 's PR, which has offered barely the tiniest morsels of information on the most anticipated game of all time. Mostly, though, they exploited us; our boredom, our doomscrolling, the way we feed on third-hand glimpses of culture like a ravenous school of piranhas.

GTA 6 wasn't the only victim of this tendency in the past week. Insomniac Games rolled out hands-on previews of Marvel's Wolverine — a studio and game that had themselves been the victims of a devastating leak three years ago. It should have been a proud, hard-earned unveiling of the real thing, but instead, the internet quickly set about demolishing a game the vast majority of people haven’t actually played.

Giovanni Colantonio teases apart the web of online controversy Insomniac is enmeshed in

Has Insomniac been more focused on making a good Wolverine experience than a good video game?

The reasons for this tedious, wrongheaded controversy are multifaceted, as Gio explored in detail (not that there aren't questions to be answered about the game — I had a few in my preview). But I do think a big part of it is this summer lull. We just don't have enough actual new stuff to think and talk about.

There might be more game releases than ever, but there hasn't been anything genuinely big and new since late May, give or take a Halo or Assassin's Creed remake; even the big franchises are feeding on themselves.

The good news is that we're about to be back. Next week is Gamescom, which usually generates a fair bit of news and a torrent of hands-on impressions of actual, playable code; and, on Thursday, Rockstar will set the record straight with the first official GTA 6 gameplay, which will probably wipe the leak from all our memories.

articles.title: Open and move windows between displays automatically
articles.subtitle: When I was visiting my pal Myke Hurley in London last year, I noticed that he had a second display to the right of his main one.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
When I was visiting my pal Myke Hurley in London last year, I noticed that he had a second display to the right of his main one. It was large and mounted vertically, and when he recorded a podcast, he kept all his recording information over there. I liked the idea of monitoring my recordings while they were going on, just for extra peace of mind, and a second display seemed like the right way to do it.

If only I had a second display! But I do, of course, because my main Mac is now a MacBook Pro. So I’ve taken to recording podcasts using the “Hurley Method,” with my Audio Hijack windows positioned on the laptop display, off to my left.

It’s nice, but if you know me, I quickly became frustrated by the number of clicks and drags I needed to perform every single time I record a podcast: Open up my laptop, open Audio Hijack, open the list of recording sessions, double-click on the one I’m using right now, then drag the window over to the laptop display.

So today I automated it.

None of my automations work if I haven’t opened the laptop, and while it sits next to my Mac in a nice stand from Twelve South, it’s closed most of the time. So my first step before moving windows to the laptop display is to make sure that the display is available! Fortunately, there’s a command-line command for that:

If you want, you can simplify the output by piping it through a grep command like system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType | grep -B1 "Resolution", but all I really want to do is search for the text string “Built-in”, which indicates that the laptop is open and its built-in display is running.

I automate most of my recording stuff using Keyboard Maestro macros triggered by an Elgato Stream Deck. So I built my automation into an existing macro in Keyboard Maestro, just adding a new if/then statement: If the calculation `SCREENCOUNT() > 1 returns true.

Then the macro runs the shell script, saves that to a local variable called LocalScreens, and it’s time for one more if/then statement, to ensure that this part of the macro only runs when more than one screen is attached and when the internal MacBook Pro display is active.

Unfortunately, the next step requires automating Audio Hijack, and while that app is very scriptable via JavaScript, and controllable via Shortcuts (or a plain text file?!), there’s no direct method of automating it from within Keyboard Maestro. So I created a basic Shortcut containing the JavaScript required to tell Audio Hijack to open a specific session by name, with the name passed to the Shortcut as input:

Then it’s a one-step item in Keyboard Maestro to run that shortcut with the name of my Audio Hijack session as the input:

(I wish this was cleaner and I didn’t need to run a shortcut. The alternative is to literally write out a text file containing the JavaScript and run it via a shell script. Is that cleaner? Doesn’t feel like it, but it’s more self-contained and doesn’t rely on the good graces of Shortcuts.)

Now that I know that my MacBook Pro display is open and my Audio Hijack session window is open, it’s a one-step command in Keyboard Maestro to make the move:

This one’s a little tricky. I have to use the Move and Resize Window command, but instead of standard numerical values, I need to use custom “smart” values that Keyboard Maestro supports.

In this case, horizontally it’s SCREENVISIBLE(Internal,MidX)-600 —essentially, 600 pixels to the left of the midpoint of the internal display—and vertically it’s SCREENVISIBLE(Internal,MidY)-250 —250 pixels up from the midpoint of the display. You can play around with the dimensions until the window ends up in the right spot, and of course, at the right size.

And that was it. Now, when I press my recording button on my Stream Deck, if my laptop display is open, the session window will automatically pop open on my laptop display. I sure do like it when things happen on my computer automatically.

articles.title: Wispr Flow takes on AI meeting assistants with Notetaker, its first product beyond dictation
articles.subtitle: Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.

Wispr Notetaker now available for Mac

If you’re unfamiliar with Wispr Flow, it is one of the leading voice-to-text AI tools for a growing number of users who feel comfortable using voice to compose messages, emails, documents, and other text instead of typing.

Granted, voice-based interactions are not practical in every environment. Still, Wispr Flow ’s rapidly growing user base (which the company said in March was expanding by 40% month over month) suggests that AI-powered dictation tools may become mainstream faster than many expected, or give them credit for.

Until now, Wispr has offered a single product, which polishes up messy speech and turns it into “clear, polished writing in every app.”

Today, the company is expanding its lineup with Notetaker, a smart, AI-powered meeting assistant, transcriber, and summarizer. The new tool is built directly into Wispr Flow and appears as a new item in the app’s left-hand sidebar.

As Wispr CEO and co-founder Tanay Kothari notes (no pun intended):

“Nobody reads meeting transcripts. But everyone acts on them. The transcript feeds the summary, the summary feeds the follow-up email, the recap goes to whoever missed the call. You’ve learned to give the notes a quick once-over before trusting them, because sometimes a name is wrong or an action item is assigned to the wrong person.”

In other words, while the transcript itself may have limited value to some, accurately extracting the key details, decisions, and action items from it can be more useful to a broader set of users.

Notetaker also briefs users before meetings by gathering relevant information from their notes and the web, with each line linked to its source. More broadly, it draws context from calendars and connected apps such as Slack.

During meetings, Notetaker provides a live transcript so the user can quickly check back on what was said. Once the meeting ends, it processes the full recording again with additional context, which Wispr says improves the final transcript and the summaries, decisions, key dates, and action items generated from it.

Afterward, users can ask questions about their full meeting history, with answers linked to the moment when the relevant information was discussed. Notetaker can also catch users up on portions of a meeting they missed or were not paying attention to.

In addition to sharing Wispr Flow ’s custom dictionary, which helps with accuracy for acronyms, names, product names, and beyond, Wispr Notetaker “draws on the apps you connect, like Slack, and your calendar, to understand what this particular conversation is about,” says Kothari.

This also helps with automatic speaker attribution, which is particularly useful for meetings with several participants.

Wispr Notetaker transcribes meetings based on on-device audio capture, rather than joining calls as a separate participant.

It works across multiple meeting platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, and Slack huddles, and has MCP support, allowing users to pull transcripts, summaries, and notes into Claude, ChatGPT, and custom agents or workflows.

Wispr Notetaker is available beginning today on Mac, with a Windows version in development.

articles.title: 30 Years Ago, One Console and Two Games Changed My Life
articles.subtitle: Without my Nintendo epiphany, I wouldn't be writing about games 30 years later Switchboard is Polygon's weekly newsletter for all things Nintendo, sent on Thursdays and published on the site on Saturdays. You can subscribe here. This Sunday, Aug.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Without my Nintendo epiphany, I wouldn't be writing about games 30 years later

Switchboard is Polygon's weekly newsletter for all things Nintendo, sent on Thursdays and published on the site on Saturdays. You can subscribe here.

This Sunday, Aug. 23, is the 35th anniversary of the release of the Super Nintendo Entertainment System in North America. We'll be celebrating the console with a series of articles on Polygon over the weekend, so I'm not going to dive too deep into its brilliance, or the generational hot streak that it inspired in Nintendo's in-house studios, here. But I thought I'd share a personal perspective on it.

I grew up with the video games of the 1980s home computer scene in the U. K. ; my foundational texts were the likes of Manic Miner, the early works of Rare (then called Ultimate Play the Game), and the homebrew aesthetic of solo coders like Jeff Minter. I largely missed the 16-bit era in my teens because my family couldn't afford a new computer or console.

I remember yearning for an Atari ST and coveting my best friend's Sega Genesis (called the Mega Drive over here). I drifted away from games and got into movies. I had basically no contact with Nintendo at all.

Then, when I was at university in the mid-'90s, my roommate bought an old, used SNES. At that point, the console was at the end of its life — PlayStation had just launched, and Nintendo 64 was around the corner. But it was new to me. My friend got two games with it, Super Mario World and Super Mario Kart.

I simply couldn't believe these two games. I was astonished. It's not that I was totally out of touch with the medium; I knew there'd been far more graphically rich games in the past few years, and I understood that 3D was about to happen. Super Mario World and Super Mario Kart looked pretty simple, even then.

Bear in mind, though, that I'd never played a Shigeru Miyamoto-designed game before, or experienced game software that had been through Nintendo's famously rigorous testing. The two games married an incredibly tactile, almost physical solidity with design that was at once abstract, intricate, and mischievous. Their childish simplicity betrayed an ocean of sophistication and depth that could be explored — and even felt — with just a handful of basic digital inputs.

Super Mario World stunned me by the way it kept inventing new rulesets, then breaking, subverting, or discarding them. And Super Mario Kart … well, we played it every single day for a year, my friend and I finessing our driving skills into a finely pointed rivalry as we slid expertly around courses made of chocolate mud.

I'll never forget it. This pair of SNES classics reawakened my love of video games and vastly expanded my understanding of the medium's potential for invention and finesse. Without them, I wouldn't have had this career or be writing to you now. I soon had a PlayStation (or my girlfriend did, anyway), was reading Edge magazine, was exploring the Nintendo back catalog, and was eagerly anticipating the N64, Super Mario 64, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

A whole world opened up to me. But I still think — if you take personal context into account, and how can you not — that Super Mario World and Super Mario Kart are the two greatest video games I have ever played.

eShop game of the week: Duskfade

Relive the cute-but-serious PS2 era of Kingdom Hearts and Jak and Daxter with this expert tribute from developer Weird Beluga. They don't make action-platformers like this anymore. " Duskfade is a wonderful time. It never overstays its welcome. It's wholesome, funny, somewhat challenging at times, and it rewards exploration. It’s a nostalgia bullseye," wrote Ford James in Polygon's review.

Nintendo Classics game of the week: Panel de Pon

You probably know this game as Tetris Attack; this is the original Japanese release, without the Mario characters and the Tetris licence that Nintendo of America rather mercenarily slapped on it. Anyway, it's an unfussy and absolutely superb match-three puzzle game by Intelligent Systems of Fire Emblem and Paper Mario fame. One of the SNES' best.

Nintendo Music track of the week: "Title Screen" from Super Metroid

The SNES' Super Metroid has one of the most evocative and atmospheric title screens of all time: a Metroid pulses in captivity in a lab, the floor scattered with scientists' corpses. It's made all the more unforgettable by this chilling, minimalist loop of pulsing bass, ominous synth, and strange breathing sounds.

OpenAI is expanding privacy protections for eligible API customers with Zero Data Retention for its frontier AI models, while also testing a new Private Safety Processing system that checks for harmful activity without giving company personnel access to customer prompts or model responses.

Under Zero Data Retention, OpenAI says it does not retain prompts or outputs after processing a request, customer content remains unavailable for employee review, and enterprise data does not train its models unless a customer explicitly opts in.

The policy targets companies working with financial records, health information, confidential business plans, proprietary research, and other sensitive data where storage periods and internal access require strict controls.

Set us as a preferred source and our Apple reporting ranks higher in your Google Search results and Discover feed — one tap, no account changes.

Private Safety Processing adds automated monitoring

OpenAI says some forms of misuse only become clear across several related interactions, especially when users repeatedly test safeguards, coordinate activity across accounts, or carry out longer agent-based tasks.

“Private Safety Processing extends those protections across related interactions, allowing automated systems to identify patterns without OpenAI personnel having access to retained customer content.”

OpenAI says customer-controlled Zero Data Retention deployments keep content on infrastructure managed by the customer, while another planned option will store encrypted content on OpenAI infrastructure using customer-controlled keys.

When automated systems identify potential misuse, OpenAI receives a limited safety signal describing the category and severity of the activity rather than the original prompts or responses.

Customers can review alerts through their own records and choose whether to share additional information during an appeal or verified abuse investigation.

OpenAI is testing Private Safety Processing with early customers and plans to begin rolling it out in September, alongside a technical white paper covering its architecture and safeguards.

articles.title: Apple’s upcoming headphones appear to be built for MacBook Neo users
articles.subtitle: Macworld For the second time this week, an unreleased Apple product has been leaked in shockingly thorough fashion. After a video demonstrating camera-equipped AirPods was spotted in macOS 26.7 on Monday, the Beats 360 over-ears headphones have now been...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
For the second time this week, an unreleased Apple product has been leaked in shockingly thorough fashion. After a video demonstrating camera-equipped AirPods was spotted in macOS 26.7 on Monday, the Beats 360 over-ears headphones have now been revealed on multiple retail websites despite not yet officially existing.

The headphones were spotted by Redditors on Amazon U.K., and one user going by the handle HappyMcPe promptly started a thread featuring more than half a dozen photos of the device. They were also spotted on other retail sites such as Apcom Slovakia and Misco, but all the listings now appear to have been taken down.

Based on the images–which we would tend to assume are legitimate, since they were used by multiple legitimate retailers and have been guiltily taken down since being spotted–the new headphones have a noticeably different design from the two currently available Beats over-ears. Unlike the Studio Pro and Solo 4, the Beats 360 has a separate padded section on the underside of the headpiece, as well as much more of an open mesh on the earcups.

Elsewhere in the listings it’s made clear that the padded section can be detached, as can the cushions over the ears, and that these are available separately as an Extra Cushion Kit. There seems to be two versions of the cushion: Performance Knit and UltraPlush.

The images also make it apparent that these are the same unreleased headphones which football star Lamine Yamal was seen with in multiple Instagram posts earlier this summer.

While we’re discussing design, it’s worth mentioning that the color finishes are very MacBook Neo-coded. The 360 is available in Sky, Black, Navy, Cloud, Pink, and Volt (a bright neon yellow and a good match for the Neo’s Citrus finish). That’s way more options, incidentally, than the Studio Pro, which comes in four colors, or the Solo 4, which comes in three.

But the leak spills far more beans than simply what the new headphones look like. We’ve got pricing, for example: £331.99 on Misco, and $299 in the DataVision listing.

In fact, product descriptions reveal almost everything about the new headphones. They offer active noise cancellation (“up to 1. 75x more noise cancellation” than the Beats Studio Pro, the description claims), though they don’t appear to feature an H2 or indeed any other Apple chip. They are rated as IPX4 for water and sweat resistance. They’re compatible with both Apple and Android products.

They have all-day battery life even with ANC enabled. They can be folded flat. They come with a “woven ripstop fabric carrying case. ”

It’s another huge leak, in other words. We don’t know when the headphones will come out, but based on the number of retail companies that had the information, we’d guess it’ll be soon. Watch this space in the coming days for any remaining details that weren’t accidentally leaked today.

articles.title: OpenAI explains what will happen when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend
articles.subtitle: It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.

ChatGPT is the new ChatGPT Atlas

As we reported in July, OpenAI is discontinuing its standalone Atlas browser in favor of browser tools built into the new ChatGPT desktop app. Atlas is scheduled to stop working on August 9 following a brief wind-down period.

OpenAI warns that Atlas may no longer open, browse, or support agentic workflows after that date. Because the discontinued browser will not continue receiving security updates, users will want to move to a supported alternative.

The transition may require some manual housekeeping for some. Atlas bookmarks will not transfer automatically. OpenAI recommends exporting bookmarks as an HTML file and saving important pages before Sunday’s deadline.

Cookies may have export options where available. ChatGPT conversation history is stored separately and will remain available.

AI browser alternatives

OpenAI is directing users toward the new ChatGPT desktop app. Its built-in browser supports multiple tabs, downloads, website logins, autofill, password management, extensions, and persistent browser state. However, it’s not exactly a browser-first experience.

The company recommends its Chrome extension when a task requires an existing Chrome profile, signed-in session, open tabs, or other extensions. ChatGPT’s desktop app also includes a “computer use” functionality that can optionally let it control Safari when granted permission.

There are plenty of other AI browser options on the Mac, including Comet, Dia, Opera Neon, and Aside. Anthropic is taking a similar two-track approach: Claude Code offers a sandboxed in-app browser, while its Chrome extension can work with existing logged-in sessions.

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

Privacy is core

articles.title: Dishonored was a last-ditch effort by Arkane Studios after years of fruitless contract work, according to the game's co-creator: 'I think we had four months of money left'
articles.subtitle: "We were farming out people left and right."
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Former Arkane Austin head Harvey Smith recently announced his new studio, Black Pony Immersive. As the name suggests will be dedicated to making immersive sims in the tradition of Deus Ex and System Shock. It's a commitment that I wholeheartedly support, though as is always the case with this genre, there's a concern over whether such a move is commercially viable.

As it turns out, however, this isn't the first time that Smith has bet the house on an immersive sim and come up trumps. That's exactly what happened with Dishonored —the game that cemented Arkane's reputation as the new guardian of this particular strand of RPG.

Speaking to The Game Business, Smith revealed that Dishonored was a ride or die project, a way out of a mire of fruitless contract work for other developers. "People would come tell us 'Man, to keep the business alive, you better take some contracts. You need to be working on whatever you can get.' And for a while we tried that, even though it felt wrong."

Despite some promising projects like a cancelled Half-Life 2 episode, Smith's fears proved justified: "There was a point in time when Arkane was about to go under. I think we had four months of money left. We were working on Boom Blox with EA. We were pitching to Ubisoft. We had a couple of guys on a zombie shooter. We were farming people out left and right. We were on nine projects at once."

Eventually, Arkane decided to stop simply taking on third-party projects just to survive and create what they wanted come hell or high water. "At some point, we realised this is not the way. We are here to do a very specific thing. Let's focus on that, and let's go under if that's what is going to happen. Instead, the result was Dishonored, which was one of the big turnarounds of my career."

This experience reinforced Smith's belief that the best chance of succeeding in the games industry is to make what you're truly passionate about. As such, Black Pony Immersive has already stated that it won't chase trends —attempting which produced Arkane's one true misfire Redfall —and ignore the fears of the wider industry that results in an aversion to creative risk.

Naturally, I can't wait to see what Smith's renewed commitment to immersive sims results in. Between this, New Blood's ongoing development of Gloomwood and Fallen Aces, and the unnamed first-person RPG from WolfEye studios—founded by Arkane's co-founder Raphaël Colantonio —we may finally be headed out of the 'it's so over' phase of the immersive sim's life-cycle.

articles.title: ChatGPT Can Now Read and Send iMessages on Mac
articles.subtitle: OpenAI today said there's a new Apple Messages plugin for ChatGPT, allowing ChatGPT on Mac to search messages, draft messages, analyze conversations, and send replies to people.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
OpenAI today said there's a new Apple Messages plugin for ChatGPT, allowing ChatGPT on Mac to search messages, draft messages, analyze conversations, and send replies to people.

The Apple Messages plugin can be installed from the ChatGPT Plugins interface, and it is listed under Public. OpenAI suggests users try these prompts:

Check my calendar and reply to [name] with a few times I'm free for dinner next week

Suggest follow ups from yesterday in messages

Find birthdays in @messages and add them to my calendar

Find potential spam messages I can delete

ChatGPT can access iMessages, SMS messages, and RCS messages. Sending a message requires user approval by default, and OpenAI warns against granting persistent approval. For the Messages integration to work, ChatGPT needs Full Disk Access in System Settings, as well as access to contact names and automation tools.

Apple's involvement in the plugin's development is unknown, but it uses AppleScript and Accessibility settings to function on a Mac. Apple and OpenAI are currently facing off in court after Apple sued OpenAI over theft of trade secrets.

Messages integration is available in ChatGPT Work and Codex in the desktop version of ChatGPT, but it does not work in regular ChatGPT chats. It is available for all ChatGPT users who have an Apple silicon Mac.

articles.title: Pastebot 3 Doubles Down on Mac Clipboard Automation and Introduces Two New Business Models
articles.subtitle: Pastebot’s Quick Menu. Tapbots has released Pastebot 3, a ground-up rewrite of the Mac clipboard manager that includes several powerful automation and customization options, along with two new pricing models.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Pastebot’s Quick Menu.

Tapbots has released Pastebot 3, a ground-up rewrite of the Mac clipboard manager that includes several powerful automation and customization options, along with two new pricing models.

Pastebot was already one of the Mac’s best clipboard utilities, capable of managing an extensive collection of copied text and images in multiple formats, PDFs, URLs, files, and HTML, along with metadata. The app can handle up to 1,500 clippings and features fast search, extensive customizable keyboard shortcuts, list and detail views of clipboard items, and iCloud sync between multiple Macs.

Pastebot 3’s main menu.

What sets Pastebot 3 apart is its addition of deep automation tools. Not only does the update add MCP support, making it an excellent tool to use with Claude or ChatGPT/Codex, but it includes a brand new CLI that you or an agent can use from Terminal or incorporate into scripts you build. Commands include:

List available Pastebins

Browse and search clipboard history

Filter results by Pastebin or date

Retrieve the full text of a clipping

Retrieve images from clippings

List available Pastebot filters

Apply filters to clippings or supplied text

Place an existing clipping on the clipboard

Create new text or image clippings

Paste clipboard contents into the frontmost app

Delete individual clippings

Clear the main clipboard history

Filters.
